_meta.status: draft - needs review by a gynecologist and a nutritionist before launch

grades.strong: large cohorts or consistent systematic reviews
grades.moderate: systematic reviews of small or low-quality trials, or one large RCT
grades.personal: research does not support a general rule; the app learns it from her own check-ins

menstrual.title: Menstrual phase
menstrual.summary: Your period. The uterine lining sheds. For most people this lasts about 4-7 days.

tips.text: Cramps, lower back ache and tiredness are common now. Note how bad they are each day so you can see your pattern.
A heat pad or hot water bottle on your lower belly can ease cramps. In trials it worked about as well as, or better than, common painkillers.
Gentle movement is fine if you feel like it. Rest is fine too. Exercise done regularly through the whole month is what's linked to less period pain.
Relaxation exercises, stretching and yoga reduced period pain in trials and had the lowest dropout.
Heavy periods are a common cause of low iron. Iron-rich foods (red meat, lentils, beans, leafy greens) plus vitamin C help. If you feel very tired or dizzy, ask a doctor to check your iron.
Ginger tea is a nice option. Ginger powder (750-2000 mg) in the first 3-4 days eased cramps in small trials. Ask a pharmacist before taking supplements.
Sleep often feels worst around your period. An earlier night or a lighter evening can help.
Energy is often lower now, but it's different for everyone. Your check-ins will show what your period is like for you.

follicular.title: Follicular phase
follicular.summary: After your period ends, estrogen rises as your body gets ready to ovulate. This phase changes length the most from cycle to cycle.

tips.text: This is the part of your cycle that stretches or shrinks the most, which is why your period date can move around.
Train the way that feels right. Research hasn't found that you should train harder or easier in a particular phase, so your own energy is the better guide.
No special diet is needed for this phase. Keep up iron-rich foods if your period was heavy.
Many people feel their energy pick up after their period ends. Your check-ins will show if that's true for you.

ovulation.title: Ovulation (estimated)
ovulation.summary: An egg is released. This is an estimate: ovulation can move by several days between cycles, so don't use it for birth control.

tips.text: Only about 1 in 4 women always ovulate between days 10 and 17, so treat this window as a rough guide.
After ovulation your body temperature goes up a little and stays higher until your next period.
No phase-specific training rule is backed by research. Go by how you feel today.

luteal.title: Luteal phase
luteal.summary: After ovulation, progesterone rises. It usually lasts about 12 days and ends when your period starts.

tips.text: Feeling hungrier, or craving chocolate, sweets or salt, is common late in this phase. It's normal, not a lack of willpower.
Regular meals with protein and fibre can help with cravings. Protein intake tends to go up naturally in this phase.
About 1 in 4 women get PMS (20-32%) and 3-8% get the more severe PMDD. Many women notice no mood change at all. Your check-ins will show your own pattern.
If PMS hits you hard, calcium is one of the better-studied options: in one large trial, symptoms dropped 48% vs 30% on placebo. Talk to a doctor before starting supplements.
Bloating and breast tenderness can show up before your period. Magnesium helped these in one small trial, after 2 months.
Your body runs a little warmer now, so a cooler bedroom may help you sleep.
Keep moving if it feels good. Regular exercise across the month is linked to less period pain next time.
Some women feel lower energy or more irritable before their period, many don't. After 2 cycles of check-ins, Femalogy will tell you what this phase is usually like for you.

red_flags.text: You haven't logged a period in over 90 days. Please check in with a doctor.
Soaking through a pad or tampon every hour, or passing large clots, is worth getting checked by a doctor.
Pain that stops you doing normal things, or doesn't ease with painkillers, should be checked by a doctor.
Your cycle length has been changing a lot. That can be normal, but if it keeps happening, mention it to a doctor.

disclaimer: Femalogy gives general information, not medical advice. Phase dates are estimates and must not be used for contraception.
